planting.note: Plant container-grown or bare-root shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this open, loosely branched species tolerates poor, dry, and eroded sites better than most garden shrubs and is often used to stabilize disturbed slopes.

directions: Native across a wide swath of eastern Asia, this is the tall, loosely arching species from which many named bush clover cultivars are ultimately traced. It produces slender, rose-purple pea flowers along new wood from mid to late summer, followed by small flat seedpods that persist into winter and feed songbirds and gamebirds. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it builds soil fertility on lean or eroded ground and was widely planted in the mid-20th century for exactly that purpose, though gardeners in warmer regions should watch for self-sown seedlings and remove spent flower heads before pods mature if spread is a concern. Give it an open, sunny spot with room to arch outward, and cut old stems back hard in late winter to keep new growth vigorous and floriferous.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Gibraltar Bush Clover (Compact Rosy-Pink Thunberg Lespedeza)

planting.note: Divide or root cuttings from established plants and set out in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Gibraltar regrows from the crown each year to a smaller, more manageable size than typical thunbergii seedlings, so cut the whole plant near the ground in late winter before new shoots emerge.

directions: Gibraltar was singled out by plantsman Bill Frederick around 1990 on the grounds of the historic Gibraltar estate in Wilmington, Delaware, and it remains the most commonly sold bush clover cultivar in American nurseries. It carries unusually vivid rosy-purple pea flowers in long, drooping racemes that gather into pendulous panicles, opening from late summer into fall on bluish-green trifoliate foliage. Because it dies back to a woody crown each winter and pushes rapid new growth the following season, a single plant can reach five feet or more by bloom time even though it is cut nearly to the ground annually. Its shorter, tidier stature compared with wild-type thunbergii makes it easier to place in a mixed border rather than reserving it for the back of a bed.

common_name: White Fountain Bush Clover (White-Flowered Thunberg Lespedeza)

planting.note: Propagate by division or cuttings and plant in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; White Fountain spreads quite wide relative to its height, so give it a generous open spot and cut stems to the ground in late winter to renew growth.

directions: White Fountain was found and named by Nancy Goodwin at Montrose, her North Carolina garden, after she noticed it held its clear white color and bloomed earlier and more reliably than the older white bush clover selection sold as 'Albiflora'. Weeping branches clothed in deep green trifoliate leaflets arch outward under the weight of dense racemes of small white pea flowers in late summer, creating a broad, low fountain of bloom rather than an upright shrub form. It reaches full size within about two growing seasons from a young plant and, once established, tolerates considerable drought while still attracting bees looking for late-season nectar. Because it dies back to the crown in winter in most of its range, treat it as a herbaceous perennial and cut it down before spring growth resumes.

common_name: Little Volcano Bush Clover (Compact Ryukyu Islands Lespedeza)

planting.note: Propagate by division or cuttings, since this selection is sterile and sets no seed; plant in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun, and cut the entire plant to the ground in late winter as it flowers only on new wood.

directions: Little Volcano was selected from stock originating in the Ryukyu Islands of southern Japan and stands out among bush clover cultivars for its intensely saturated purple-pink flower color, packed so densely along the arching stems from midsummer into late fall that the sage-green foliage nearly disappears beneath the bloom. Unlike seed-grown Lespedeza, it sets no viable seed, which removes the self-sowing weediness that troubles some bush clovers in warmer regions. In colder parts of its range the top growth dies back over winter regardless of pruning, so treat it as a die-back perennial and expect vigorous, fountain-shaped regrowth each spring. Established plants tolerate dry spells well and reward only minimal care beyond an annual hard cutback.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Heavenly Blue Bluebeard (Fragrant Periwinkle Compact Caryopteris)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun, ideally against a warm wall or open bed; Heavenly Blue is one of the older named caryopteris selections and remains a reliable, compact, freely flowering choice.

directions: Raised at Wayside Gardens in Ohio in the early 1950s, Heavenly Blue is among the longest-established caryopteris cultivars still in wide circulation, valued for smothering itself in fragrant, periwinkle-blue flower clusters from late summer well into fall. The toothed, grey-green leaves release an aromatic scent when brushed and stay clean through the season, and the shrub keeps a tidy, arching, rounded shape without staking or shearing during the growing season. Bees and butterflies work the late flowers heavily, making it a dependable late-nectar source when many other border shrubs have already finished. Because it flowers on new wood, cut the whole plant back hard to a few inches above ground in late winter or early spring to keep it compact and encourage the heaviest bloom.

common_name: Arthur Simmonds Bluebeard (Original Hardy Hybrid Caryopteris)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Arthur Simmonds is reported to be among the hardiest of the x clandonensis cultivars, so it is a reasonable choice for gardeners near the cold edge of caryopteris range.

directions: This cultivar is the namesake of the entire Caryopteris x clandonensis group: gardener Arthur Simmonds discovered it as a chance seedling in his garden at Clandon, near Guildford, England, in 1930, after collecting seed intending to raise Caryopteris mongholica but instead capturing an accidental cross with a nearby Caryopteris incana. Clusters of bright violet-blue flowers cover the low, arching stems from midsummer into fall above grey-green, fragrant, deer-resistant foliage, drawing steady traffic from bees and butterflies. It quickly earned Royal Horticultural Society recognition after its introduction and is still noted among clandonensis selections for its comparatively good winter hardiness. Grow it in full sun and lean, well-drained soil, and cut the plant back hard each late winter since bloom forms only on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Plant in spring in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species tolerates far colder winters and drier, sandier ground than the more common clandonensis hybrids it helped create, making it useful where those hybrids struggle.

directions: Native to the arid steppe and semi-desert margins of Mongolia and northern China, this is the northernmost and most cold-tolerant species in the genus, and it was one of the two parent species behind the accidental cross that produced the popular Caryopteris x clandonensis hybrids. In the wild it helps anchor shifting sand and stabilize dry slopes, and in the garden that same toughness translates into strong drought tolerance and reliable performance in lean, fast-draining soil where richer hybrids sulk. Slender grey-green leaves back small clusters of violet-blue, occasionally pink-tinged flowers held on wiry stems from late summer into fall. Give it full sun and avoid heavy, wet soils, and expect a looser, more open habit than the tidier named clandonensis cultivars bred from it.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
